phrases.literal: 'that', introducing the content of the seeing

phrases.english: the evil of the human was great on the earth

phrases.english: and every inclination of the thoughts of his heart
phrases.literal: 'and-every formation-of thoughts-of his-heart'; a chain of three constructs

grammar: וַיַּרְא is a wayyiqtol; כִּי introduces the object clause: what the LORD saw.
רַבָּה רָעַת הָאָדָם: the predicate adjective comes first, and the verb 'to be' is not written. רָעַת is the construct of רָעָה.
וְכׇל־יֵצֶר מַחְשְׁבֹת לִבּוֹ is a chain of constructs (every / inclination / of thoughts / of his heart) with no verb; רַק רַע is its predicate.
The etnaḥta on בָּאָרֶץ divides the verse: the evil on the earth, and then the inward cause.
segments.note: יֵצֶר is from יצר 'to form, shape'; Radak takes it as the desire of the heart's thinking, which forms and works out matters within the heart. The English 'inclination' follows that. הָאָדָם is 'the human', mankind generally (a collective), per decisions.

commentary.summary: Radak: of the two inclinations in a person's heart, one good and one bad, here all was bad; the desire of the heart's thought is called יֵצֶר because the heart forms and works things out within itself.
Sforno: כִּי רַבָּה רָעַת הָאָדָם refers to the past (לְשֶׁעָבַר), and the next clause to the future; this bears on tense reading, not on the English words.

apparatus: Onkelos renders the verse closely: 'and every inclination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil all day' (יִצְרָא מַחְשְׁבַת לִבֵּהּ לְחוֹד בִּישׁ כָּל יוֹמָא).

segments.english: The LORD regretted that he had made the human on the earth, and was grieved in his heart.
segments.literal: and-regretted the-LORD that-made [object-mark] the-human in-the-earth and-grieved-himself to his-heart

tokens.note: Niphal wayyiqtol of נחם: 'be sorry, rue'
perfect, anterior to the regret: 'he had made'
marks the definite direct object
Hithpael wayyiqtol: 'was pained'; the lexicon has only a single Hithp sense
construct form with 3rd masculine singular suffix; אֶל־לִבּוֹ 'to/in his heart'

phrases.literal: 'made', rendered as a pluperfect because the making precedes the regret
'to his-heart'; Rashi and Ramban take the heart as the seat of thought, so 'in his heart'

grammar: וַיִּנָּחֶם is a Niphal wayyiqtol; the stem is reflexive-passive, 'he let himself be sorry'.
וַיִּתְעַצֵּב is a Hithpael wayyiqtol, 'he pained himself'; it is the counterpart of the Niphal verb before it.
אֶל־לִבּוֹ: the phrase is literally 'to his heart', the inward place of thought and feeling.
The etnaḥta on בָּאָרֶץ divides the verse: the regret over the making, and then the grief.
segments.note: The two verbs speak of God in human terms. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Ramban all say the Torah speaks in human language, so the English keeps the verbs plain ('regretted', 'was grieved'). Rashi also records the other sense of נִחוּם: a change of intention. The English keeps 'regretted'; the second Rashi reading is recorded. בָּאָרֶץ (on the earth) modifies the making: Radak reads it as made of earth.

commentary.summary: Rashi: it was a נֶחָמָה (regret) before him that he made man among the lower beings, for had he been made from the upper beings he would have rebelled; the English adopts 'regretted' with the made-on-earth link.

Rashi, after Onkelos: 'it arose in the thought of the Place to grieve him' (the object is the human), and another reading: his thought turned from mercy to judgment, as every נִחוּם in Scripture means 'he took counsel what to do'. The English keeps 'regretted' and 'was grieved'; this alternative is kept here.

Rashi: he mourned the loss of the work of his hands, as in 'the king was grieved (נֶעֱצַב) over his son'; the narrative of R. Joshua ben Korha shows that God's foreknowledge does not remove the grief.
Ibn Ezra: it is known that God is not a human to regret; the Torah speaks in the language of humans, since a destroyer sees both what he made.

Ibn Ezra: וַיִּתְעַצֵּב אֶל לִבּוֹ is the opposite of 'the LORD rejoices in his works' (Ps 104:31); he also rejects the view that 'his heart' means the prophet, for then the text would not say אֶל after the verb.
Radak: בָּאָרֶץ means man mixed with the products of the earth, whose body is all earthly, unlike the heavenly image of God; this is why God did not regret making Noah.

apparatus: Onkelos: 'the LORD turned in his Memra because he made man on the earth, and said in his Memra to break their strength as his will' (a paraphrase that avoids saying God regretted).

segments.english: The LORD said, "I will wipe out the human whom I created from the face of the ground, from human to beast, to creeping thing, and to the birds of the sky, for I regret that I made them."

and to the birds of the sky

grammar: אֶמְחֶה is a first-person imperfect of מחה, 'wipe', and states a resolve; Rashi reads the verb as fitting dust, which water wipes out.
The list מֵאָדָם עַד־בְּהֵמָה עַד־רֶמֶשׂ וְעַד־עוֹף הַשָּׁמָיִם uses עַד for the limits of what is destroyed; the last item takes וְ.
The two clauses with כִּי form a pair: כִּי נִחַמְתִּי (Niphal) and כִּי עֲשִׂיתִם (Qal), so the regret is tied to the making.
The etnaḥta on הַשָּׁמָיִם divides the verse: the decree, and then the reason.
segments.note: The speech is addressed to no one stated. Ibn Ezra's own view is that it is joined to 'his heart' of verse 6 (the speech is inward), and Radak allows 'to Noah'; the English gives the bare 'said'. אֶת־הָאָדָם is 'the human' (mankind), per decisions. 'Whom I created' uses בָּרָא, the verb of Genesis 1, which the lexicon lists as Qal.

commentary.summary: Rashi: man is dust and God will bring water on him and wipe him out; this is why the verb is of 'wiping' (מִחוּי), which suits that image.

Rashi: the animals also corrupted their ways (Genesis Rabbah); another reading: everything was made for man, and with him gone what need is there for them. The English gives the plain list and records both reasons.
Rashi: כִּי נִחַמְתִּי means 'I have thought what to do about what I made', i.e. נִחוּם as a change of thought. The English keeps the plainer 'I regret'.

Ibn Ezra: וַיֹּאמֶר is said 'to his heart', or to the angels; some say to Noah; the correct view in his eyes is that it is joined to 'his heart' written above. The English leaves the addressee unstated.
Radak: 'the human' and not every person, since Noah and his sons remained; Genesis Rabbah on why water: the human was made only from dust, and only water wipes dust out.

apparatus: Onkelos: אֲרֵי תָבִית בְּמֵימְרִי 'for I have turned in my Memra' replaces 'I regret'.

segments.english: But Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD.

tokens.note: the vav contrasts Noah with the human of the previous verse
perfect, 3rd masculine singular, in a clause that begins with the subject
'favor, acceptance'
idiom: 'in the eyes of' means 'in the opinion of'

phrases.english: in the eyes of the LORD

grammar: וְנֹחַ מָצָא: the subject comes before the verb, so the clause is a contrast with the preceding judgment; hence 'But'.
מָצָא חֵן בְּעֵינֵי is an idiom for 'was acceptable to', literally 'found favor in the eyes of'.
The zaqef gadol on נֹחַ marks Noah as the subject standing apart, and the silluq closes the paragraph (פ).
segments.note: The vav is rendered 'But', following the contrast. The lexicon's עַיִן senses list 5 for 'in the presence of', which is the idiom's sense; the sense 2.b etc. are for other uses.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra: חֵן is from the root of 'mercy', and so תַּחֲנָה; the sense of 'finding favor' is like 'no eye had pity on you' (Ezekiel 16:5).
Ramban: all his deeds were pleasing before God, and this is set against the generation whose deeds caused grief; the next verse then says why.
Sforno: Noah's children were saved by favor, not desert, since he did not teach his generation to know God.
